paragraphs: This paper studies convex optimization when enforcing the constraint is itself expensive. Projected gradient methods repeatedly move their estimates back into the permitted region, while conditional gradient methods solve related linear optimization problems. The authors target settings where both operations take substantial time, making the number of constraint-handling operations an important computational concern.

Under a regularity condition on the constraint function, they develop methods that require fewer projections. Their general framework permits optimization with just one projection. For smooth objectives, it achieves an iteration complexity of O(1/epsilon), with further improvements available under strong convexity. This distinguishes the cost of improving the objective from the cost of enforcing feasibility.

They also obtain faster rates for objectives without strong convexity by assuming a local error bound and allowing a logarithmic number of projections. The rates depend on smoothness and growth near optimal solutions. Applications to constrained l1 minimization and distance metric learning demonstrate substantial speed improvements over earlier algorithms.
icml-2017-a-richer-theory-of-convex-cons.tldr: Under stated regularity and growth conditions, fewer projections can make constrained convex optimization faster.

paragraphs: Wasserstein loss minimization involves an optimization problem inside another optimization problem. The outer learning procedure depends on Wasserstein distances, but computing those distances already requires numerical work. Repeatedly obtaining the loss information needed for learning can therefore become a computational bottleneck, particularly when several levels of iteration are involved.

The paper proposes a stochastic approach based on simulated annealing. Its central computational component is a Gibbs sampler that approximates partial gradients for a sequence of Wasserstein losses. This supplies an inexact oracle: a procedure that provides approximate information needed by the surrounding optimization process, rather than requiring exact calculations at every call.

The authors emphasize numerical stability and the ability to warm-start the computation using earlier work. These properties matter when related calculations recur throughout training. They apply the method to optimal transport with Coulomb cost and Wasserstein non-negative matrix factorization, comparing it with entropy regularization. The abstract describes these comparisons without asserting a universal performance advantage.
icml-2017-a-simulated-annealing-based-in.tldr: A simulated annealing approach uses Gibbs sampling to approximate Wasserstein-loss gradients with numerical stability and warm-start support.

paragraphs: The paper develops a common optimization framework for recovering an unknown low-rank matrix. Its focus is computational efficiency in a nonconvex formulation: how to make progress toward the desired matrix while reducing the cost of the gradient calculations used during optimization. The approach is intended to support multiple recovery problems within one framework.

The algorithm combines projected gradient descent with a specially designed semi-stochastic gradient and variance reduction. Its guarantees require an appropriate starting estimator and restricted strong convexity and smoothness conditions. From these assumptions, the authors establish a projected gradient regularity property and prove linear convergence, together with improved computational complexity.

The framework accommodates observations both with and without noise. The authors report near-optimal or optimal sample complexity in the noiseless setting and statistical convergence rates in the noisy setting. These results connect computational progress with the amount and quality of available information. Specific examples provide theoretical and experimental support for the advantages of the general approach.
icml-2017-a-unified-variance-reduction-b.tldr: A variance-reduced projected gradient framework accelerates low-rank matrix recovery under suitable initialization and restricted regularity conditions.

paragraphs: In multi-label classification, one example can belong to several classes at once. Evaluation consequently has multiple perspectives, and a model that looks strong under one measure may look weaker under another. This paper asks how those differences relate to what a learning algorithm actually encourages during training.

The authors examine eleven performance measures through a common margin-based framework. They define two kinds of margin, called label-wise and instance-wise margins, to express different aspects of predictive separation. They then prove connections between maximizing these margins and optimizing corresponding performance measures. The contribution is a shared way to reason about several evaluation criteria while preserving their differences.

Using these definitions, the authors design a maximum-margin learning method named LIMO. Their empirical results support the theoretical connections. The practical significance is that choosing a training objective can be informed by the evaluation measure of interest: the framework explains why different margin objectives correspond to different kinds of measured performance.
icml-2017-a-unified-view-of-multi-label-.tldr: Two kinds of margin connect eleven multi-label evaluation measures and motivate the LIMO learning algorithm.

paragraphs: ADMM is used to fit models through distributed computation, but its behavior depends strongly on penalty parameters selected by the user. Those settings affect both performance and reliability. The paper treats parameter selection as a central part of the optimization method, with particular attention to the settings used by individual worker nodes.

The authors study distributed ADMM methods that allow different workers to use individually tuned parameters. This makes parameter choice local to each worker rather than a single undifferentiated decision for the distributed procedure. Their proposed method, adaptive consensus ADMM, or ACADMM, automatically adjusts these parameters without requiring the user to supervise the tuning process.

The theoretical contribution is an O(1/k) convergence rate for adaptive ADMM methods with node-specific parameters, where k counts iterations. This gives a convergence characterization for the adaptive setting studied in the paper. Together, the analysis and algorithm address the practical burden of tuning distributed optimization while retaining a stated rate of convergence.
icml-2017-adaptive-consensus-admm-for-di.tldr: ACADMM automatically tunes worker-specific penalty parameters, supported by an O(1/k) convergence analysis for adaptive distributed ADMM.

paragraphs: Newton methods offer fast convergence but can require expensive calculations at every iteration. For large optimization problems arising in machine learning, that cost can undermine their usefulness. Subsampled Newton methods and other stochastic second-order approaches reduce the work per iteration, making the relationship between approximation and convergence especially important.

The paper addresses gaps in the theoretical understanding of these efficient methods. Its main contribution is a unified framework for analyzing their local convergence properties. Local convergence concerns behavior near a solution, so the focus is on explaining how these methods progress in that regime rather than describing every stage of optimization.

According to the authors, the resulting analysis agrees with behavior seen in practical applications and resolves discrepancies in earlier theory. The significance is a more coherent account of methods that share the goal of retaining fast second-order progress while lowering iteration costs. This provides theoretical grounding for understanding their practical efficiency in large-scale optimization.
icml-2017-approximate-newton-methods-and.tldr: A unified local convergence framework explains the practical behavior of approximate Newton and related stochastic second-order methods.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks can be costly to store and run because their designs prioritize accuracy. This paper approaches compression by examining redundancy in the feature maps produced by a layer's filters. The goal is to retain the information that helps distinguish inputs while representing the layer's output more compactly.

The authors construct a feature-map transformation using a circulant matrix. This structure permits embedding a d-dimensional feature map with O(d log d) computation. They then reconfigure the filters so that the original input maps directly to the new compact representation. Thus, compression changes the network's internal mapping as well as the representation of its features.

The resulting network can preserve intrinsic information from the original model while using substantially fewer parameters. The authors report lower memory requirements for running the network and faster computation. Experiments on benchmark image datasets show advantages over the state-of-the-art methods considered. The broader contribution is to make feature-map redundancy an explicit target for portable network design.
icml-2017-beyond-filters-compact-feature.tldr: Compressing redundant feature maps and reconfiguring filters yields smaller, faster convolutional networks while preserving useful information.

paragraphs: Many supervised learning problems come in related pairs that run in opposite directions. Translation between two languages is one example; speech recognition and speech generation form another. The paper observes that the probability models for such tasks are connected, even though the two models are commonly trained independently.

Dual supervised learning trains both models together and explicitly uses their probabilistic relationship to regularize learning. Each task therefore participates in a shared training process that accounts for its connection to the other. The central idea is to make that relationship useful during model fitting, instead of treating the two prediction problems as unrelated.

The authors demonstrate that this coupled training can improve the practical performance of both tasks. Their applications include machine translation, image processing, and sentiment analysis. These findings support the value of exploiting probabilistic connections across paired tasks, while the claim remains one of demonstrated improvements in the applications studied rather than a guarantee for every possible task pair.
icml-2017-dual-supervised-learning-6104b.tldr: Jointly training paired supervised tasks with a probabilistic consistency regularizer can improve both models.

paragraphs: Latent count variables can take arbitrarily large integer values, making standard graphical-model inference algorithms unsuitable for the models studied here. Earlier work used probability generating functions to perform efficient exact inference for certain Poisson latent-variable models. However, its reliance on symbolic manipulation made extension to broader model classes uncertain.

This paper keeps the generating-function approach but changes how the required calculations are performed. Instead of manipulating symbolic expressions, the authors adapt automatic differentiation techniques to compute higher-order derivatives. These derivatives provide the information needed for inference, expanding the range of models that can be handled efficiently and exactly.

The supported class includes branching processes and autoregressive models for integer observations. This matters because it extends exact inference to structures used in areas such as population ecology and applied mathematics. Experiments show greater scalability than the approximate methods considered and demonstrate new applications. The contribution combines broader model coverage with a different computational route to exact answers.
icml-2017-exact-inference-for-integer-la.tldr: Automatic differentiation of probability generating functions expands efficient exact inference to a broader class of latent count models.

paragraphs: The paper studies estimation of the parametric part of a single-index model when the number of input dimensions is high. A central aim is to move beyond methods that require normally distributed covariates. The proposed approach allows non-Gaussian inputs while still providing a theoretical account of estimation accuracy.

Using Stein's Lemma, the authors construct estimators from the covariate distribution's score function. They also address heavy-tailed score functions and responses by carefully thresholding the empirical quantities used in estimation. Thresholding is the mechanism used to handle these potentially extreme observations, making tail behavior an explicit part of the estimator's design.

Under a bounded fourth-moment condition, the authors establish optimal statistical convergence rates. That assumption is part of the guarantee: allowing non-Gaussian and heavy-tailed variables does not mean removing all distributional requirements. Extensive numerical experiments support the theory. The contribution is therefore a combination of broader input distributions, a method for handling heavy tails, and strong statistical guarantees under a stated moment condition.
icml-2017-high-dimensional-non-gaussian-.tldr: Thresholded score-function estimators achieve optimal rates for high-dimensional non-Gaussian single-index models under a bounded fourth-moment condition.

paragraphs: Earlier text-generation results found that variational autoencoders with LSTM decoders could perform worse than simpler LSTM language models. One proposed explanation was that the decoder ignored information supplied by the encoder. This paper investigates that issue by changing how much previously generated text the decoder can use.

The authors replace the LSTM decoder with a dilated convolutional network. Adjusting its dilation architecture controls the amount of preceding context available during generation. Their experiments reveal a trade-off: a decoder's capacity to use context interacts with how effectively it uses the encoded information. Decoder design therefore becomes a way to manage the contribution of the latent representation.

When this balance is carefully managed, the authors show that their variational autoencoders outperform LSTM language models, with perplexity improvements on two datasets. They also investigate semi-supervised and unsupervised labeling, reporting gains over several strong baselines. These findings support the usefulness of controlling decoder context for both language modeling and the labeling tasks studied.
icml-2017-improved-variational-autoencod.tldr: Dilated convolutional decoders help text VAEs balance contextual capacity with use of encoded information, improving reported modeling and labeling results.

paragraphs: A dialogue agent needs both to choose what to do and to express that choice in language. The paper identifies difficulties with two existing approaches: manually defining a small action space limits scalability, while deterministic sentence models fail to represent conversational variability. It proposes learning an intermediate representation of dialogue intentions.

The Latent Intention Dialogue Model uses a discrete hidden variable within neural variational inference. This variable represents underlying intentions learned from dialogue. In goal-oriented settings, these intentions can be interpreted as actions that guide response generation. Reinforcement learning can then refine those actions autonomously, connecting learned language generation with decision-making.

Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of discrete latent variables for learning goal-oriented dialogues. The reported results exceed published benchmarks in both corpus-based and human evaluations. The significance is that the same learned intention representation supports modeling variation in conversation and directing responses toward a goal, with empirical evidence for the dialogue settings examined in the paper.
icml-2017-latent-intention-dialogue-mode.tldr: Learned discrete dialogue intentions guide response generation and can be refined through reinforcement learning for goal-oriented conversation.

paragraphs: Learning an optimizer is useful only if the resulting update rule can handle problems beyond its training examples without excessive overhead. This paper addresses both transfer to new tasks and scaling to larger models. It introduces a learned gradient descent optimizer built around a hierarchical recurrent neural network.

The architecture keeps per-parameter overhead small and incorporates features reflecting known optimization structure. Training uses an ensemble of small, diverse optimization tasks designed to capture common properties of loss landscapes. The optimizer learns to outperform RMSProp and ADAM on problems in that training corpus, establishing its effectiveness within the setting used to teach it.

The more consequential tests examine transfer. Despite receiving no neural networks in meta-training, the optimizer performs comparably or better on small convolutional networks. It also trains Inception V3 and ResNet V2 on ImageNet for thousands of steps. These results demonstrate transfer across substantial changes in task type and scale, with the large-model claim specifically covering the reported optimization runs.
icml-2017-learned-optimizers-that-scale-.tldr: A hierarchical recurrent optimizer trained on small tasks transfers to neural-network training at much larger scales with reduced overhead.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning from short event sequences whose observations are cut off at both ends. Such fragments provide incomplete temporal information, creating a challenge for estimating models of asynchronous events. The authors address the problem within the Hawkes-process framework, using sequences collected over different observation intervals.

Their method creates longer training sequences through sampling and stitching. For each observed fragment, it samples candidate predecessor and successor sequences and joins them together. This makes data synthesis the central tool for handling the incomplete observations: the training material is expanded by constructing possible surrounding sequences from available candidates.

The authors discuss why this construction is reasonable and feasible using likelihood-based arguments. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show improved learning for both time-invariant and time-varying Hawkes processes. The findings support the value of synthesized temporal context in the tested settings. They establish improvements in model learning without claiming that the stitched sequences reconstruct the actual unobserved history.
icml-2017-learning-hawkes-processes-from.tldr: Sampling and stitching short censored event sequences into longer training sequences improves the reported learning of Hawkes processes.

paragraphs: Latent space models have enough capacity to capture complex patterns, but that flexibility can also lead to overfitting. Encouraging different model components to be diverse had shown empirical promise. This paper asks for a more precise account of diversity and a theoretical explanation of its effect on generalization.

The authors describe diversity through near-orthogonality and impose constraints on the angles between components. Their analysis exposes a trade-off: increasing diversity reduces estimation error while increasing approximation error. In other words, the restriction can improve learning from limited observations while also reducing the model's ability to represent the target. The analysis therefore does not imply that more diversity is always better.

An efficient ADMM algorithm solves the resulting constrained learning problems. Experiments show improved generalization and stronger results than the other diversity-promoting approaches considered. The contribution joins a concrete geometric constraint, an optimization method, and a theoretical account of competing errors, making the benefits and costs of diversity more explicit.
icml-2017-learning-latent-space-models-w.tldr: Angular constraints improve reported generalization while revealing that greater component diversity trades lower estimation error for higher approximation error.

paragraphs: Cardinality constraints restrict how many elements a solution may select or use. They appear in sparse learning, feature selection, and compressed sensing. When several such constraints overlap, projecting an estimate into the permitted set is generally NP-hard, making a basic step of constrained optimization difficult.

The paper identifies a structured case called Three-view Cardinality Structure, or TVCS. For overlapping constraints with this structure, the authors express the projection problem as a linear program. They prove that a vertex solution of that program also solves the original projection problem, so the reformulation preserves the answer in the setting considered.

They further show that such a solution can be found with complexity proportional to the number of variables and constraints. The structural condition is central to this efficiency result; it does not cover arbitrary overlapping cardinality constraints. Synthetic experiments and applications involving gene regulatory networks and crowdsourcing validate the proposed model and method, demonstrating uses for this tractable special case.
icml-2017-on-the-projection-operator-to-.tldr: Three-view structure makes a generally hard cardinality-constrained projection solvable through a linear program with proportional computational complexity.

paragraphs: A rule list predicts through an ordered sequence of IF-THEN statements, giving it a logical structure that can be inspected directly. This paper builds probabilistic rule lists from previously mined association rules. The goal is a practical balance among predictive accuracy, simplicity, and the time needed to construct the model.

The algorithm aims to optimize over rule lists rather than rely on the greedy splitting and pruning associated with decision trees. Its efficiency comes from several complementary techniques: theoretical bounds that support practical screening or bounding, reuse of computations, and carefully optimized software libraries. Together, these reduce the computational burden of the search.

The authors report a speed improvement of two orders of magnitude over previous work. For many practical problems, the method also achieves better accuracy and sparsity than decision trees. Runtime is practical in many cases and often lower than that of decision trees. These are qualified practical findings, showing that interpretable rule-list models can be computationally competitive in the settings studied.
icml-2017-scalable-bayesian-rule-lists-2.tldr: Efficient search makes probabilistic rule-list learning substantially faster, with favorable accuracy, sparsity, and runtime on many practical problems.

paragraphs: Multi-source transfer regression uses information from several source domains to help predict in a target domain. A key difficulty is that the sources may relate to the target in different ways. This paper investigates whether Gaussian-process covariance functions can express those differing relationships effectively.

The authors analyze a family of transfer covariance functions intended to represent each source's pairwise similarity to the target. They show that, within the general Gaussian-process modeling construction studied, these functions can capture only a common similarity coefficient across sources. That restriction may lead to unsatisfactory transfer when distinct source-target relationships need to be represented.

To address the issue, they propose TC_MSStack, which combines transfer covariance functions with stacking. The design brings together the benefits of the covariance approach and an integrated combination strategy. Experiments use one synthetic dataset and two real-world datasets, with up to eleven sources in the latter settings. The reported results support the method's effectiveness for the multi-source regression problems examined.
icml-2017-source-target-similarity-model.tldr: TC_MSStack combines transfer covariance functions with stacking to address a shared-similarity restriction in multi-source Gaussian-process regression.

paragraphs: Combining sparse and group-sparse components allows a model to represent both shared structure and individual exceptions. In multi-task learning, this can accommodate parameters that overlap across tasks while preserving task-specific choices. The paper studies statistical guarantees for this flexible form of regularization in high-dimensional estimation.

Earlier consistency analyses required an incoherence assumption between the two superposed components that the authors regard as overly restrictive. They provide consistency results that remove this requirement, narrowing the gap between the models' practical success and their theoretical justification. The advance concerns the assumptions needed to support estimation guarantees, rather than a claim that all assumptions disappear.

The paper also analyzes nonconvex versions of these models. It shows that they can recover the true support set under substantially milder conditions and with fewer samples than convex counterparts. Support recovery identifies which parameters are active. Experiments illustrate why these differences may matter in practice, supporting a case for nonconvex formulations within the settings analyzed.
icml-2017-sparse-group-sparse-dirty-mode.tldr: New guarantees remove a restrictive incoherence requirement and show support-recovery advantages for nonconvex sparse-plus-group-sparse models.

paragraphs: This paper connects the shape of a convex objective near its optimal solutions with the global efficiency of stochastic optimization. Its key result uses a local growth condition rather than requiring comparable growth throughout the entire domain. Faster growth near the optimum can therefore support faster overall convergence under the stated condition.

When growth is characterized by an exponent theta between zero and one, the iteration complexity can scale as 1/epsilon raised to 2(1-theta), apart from logarithmic factors. The authors establish optimality up to at most such a factor. Their two accelerated stochastic subgradient methods repeatedly solve approximate problems inside local regions whose sizes shrink as optimization approaches the solution set.

The paper also develops practical variants that do not require knowing the multiplicative growth constant, or even theta. It identifies machine-learning problems that benefit from the theory. In particular, l1-regularized empirical objectives with polyhedral losses, including hinge and absolute loss, admit logarithmic iteration complexity for the proposed stochastic methods.
icml-2017-stochastic-convex-optimization.tldr: Local objective growth can yield near-optimal faster global convergence for stochastic convex optimization through progressively shrinking search regions.

paragraphs: Graphical-model inference can involve passing messages that become too large to handle efficiently. Tensor belief propagation tackles this problem by approximating messages within the junction tree algorithm. The paper's main idea is to use a compact representation for both the model's potential functions and the messages exchanged during inference.

Each is represented as a mixture of rank-one tensors. Their factored structure makes marginalization, which combines information over variables being removed, quick to compute. Multiplication is handled approximately through sampling. This pairing adapts the required inference operations to the compact representation, rather than relying on unrestricted message tables.

The authors derive sufficient conditions under which the algorithm performs well. These include cases involving high-treewidth graphs, where exact inference is intractable. The conditions establish favorable settings rather than a guarantee for every difficult graph. Experimental comparisons with several approximate inference methods show good performance, supporting the practicality of tensor representations for the inference problems examined.
icml-2017-tensor-belief-propagation-a86b.tldr: Compact tensor mixtures and sampled multiplication enable approximate junction-tree inference, with sufficient performance conditions and supporting experiments.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks become difficult to train when each input has very many dimensions. The input-to-hidden weight matrix grows large, creating a major obstacle for applications such as video modeling. Existing approaches reduce input dimensionality with feature extractors; this paper instead addresses the size of the mapping within the recurrent model.

The authors factorize the input-to-hidden matrix using Tensor-Train decomposition and learn the factorized representation during training. This provides a more compact way to express the large transformation that connects inputs to hidden states. The method is presented as a general approach for recurrent architectures exposed to high-dimensional sequential data.

On classification tasks across multiple real-world video datasets, the model achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art approaches while its architecture is orders of magnitude less complex. These results support the usefulness of the factorization for video classification. The authors also suggest that it could help bring expressive recurrent architectures from other domains into high-dimensional sequence modeling.
icml-2017-tensor-train-recurrent-neural-.tldr: Tensor-Train factorization greatly reduces recurrent-network complexity while retaining competitive reported performance on video classification.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction and clustering are often performed one after the other, even though the representation chosen in the first step shapes the clusters available in the second. This paper pursues joint learning so that the reduced representation and K-means clustering can influence each other during optimization.

The authors assume that observed data arise from cluster-friendly latent representations through an unknown, potentially nonlinear transformation. They use a deep neural network for dimensionality reduction to accommodate this more flexible relationship. The motivation is to retain the benefits of joint optimization while expanding beyond approaches based on a linear relationship between latent representations and observations.

The paper designs both the network structure and a joint optimization objective, then develops an effective, scalable algorithm for the resulting problem. Experiments on several real datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution is a way to learn representations with clustering explicitly in mind, using nonlinear modeling capacity to address a broader class of underlying data-generation relationships.
icml-2017-towards-k-means-friendly-space.tldr: Jointly learning a deep representation and K-means clusters accommodates nonlinear relationships between observations and cluster-friendly latent spaces.

paragraphs: Latent space models aim to uncover hidden patterns in observed data. The paper focuses on two challenges: representing uncommon patterns when frequencies are imbalanced, and reducing model size while preserving expressive power. Both motivate encouraging diversity among the components that make up the model's hidden representation.

The proposed regularizer combines uncorrelation with evenness. Uncorrelation encourages components to carry less overlapping information, while evenness encourages them to play similarly important roles in modeling the data. The authors express this joint goal by encouraging the component covariance matrix to have more uniform eigenvalues, providing a mathematical target for the desired diversity.

They apply the regularizer to two latent space models and develop an efficient optimization algorithm. Experiments involving healthcare, image, and text data demonstrate its effectiveness. The distinctive contribution is to treat diversity as both separation among components and balance in their contributions, bringing the two considerations into a single regularization approach motivated by compactness and coverage of infrequent patterns.
icml-2017-uncorrelation-and-evenness-a-n.tldr: A diversity regularizer encourages latent components to be uncorrelated and similarly influential by making covariance eigenvalues more uniform.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning tasks are usually described as Markov decision processes, but a specification can entangle how the environment behaves with what the learner is trying to achieve. This makes task descriptions harder to generalize and can obscure connections between settings such as episodic and continuing learning.

The paper introduces an RL task formalism intended to make these relationships clearer and task specification more modular. Its constructs include a generalization of transition-based discounting. Through a series of examples, the authors show how the formalism can represent different task settings within a common framework, illustrating both its breadth and its practical usefulness.

They also extend standard learning machinery, including Bellman operators, and theoretical results such as approximation-error bounds. This matters because a new task description becomes more useful when established tools for learning and analysis carry over to it. The result is a mathematically grounded foundation intended to support further theory and simplify the use and development of reinforcement-learning algorithms.
icml-2017-unifying-task-specification-in.tldr: A modular RL task formalism unifies task settings and extends familiar learning operators and theoretical guarantees.
